alt: Two topic areas. Theories of the family and social change (3.1 perspectives, 3.2 diversity and change) links to power, control and resistance; socialisation, culture and identity; and social change and development. Family roles and changing relationships (4.1 gender, 4.2 age) links to power, control and resistance and to inequality and opportunity.
caption: Paper 2 has two topic areas, four sub-topics and four linked key concepts.

after: ## 3.1 Perspectives on the role of the family
alt: Three cards: functionalists say the family benefits members and society, with a debate about loss of functions; Marxists say it benefits capitalism through ideological control, reproduction of labour and consumption; feminists challenge both for overlooking inequality within the family.
caption: Functionalists see benefits for society, Marxists for capitalism, and feminists see hidden inequality.

alt: Five family and household forms: nuclear, extended, lone-parent, reconstituted and single-person. The New Right sees growing diversity as a social problem; postmodernists see it as greater individual choice. Students also examine whether the nuclear family remains dominant and how social policy shapes family form.
caption: The New Right sees diversity as a problem; postmodernists see it as choice.

after: ## 4.1 Gender equality and experiences of family life
alt: Four areas of conjugal roles: housework, childcare, power and emotion work. Liberal, radical and Marxist feminists offer different explanations of inequality within the family. Below, a line from positive to negative experience shows that whether family life is good for its members is a live debate.
caption: Conjugal roles span housework, childcare, power and emotion work; feminists disagree on why they are unequal.

alt: Four cards on age and family life: childhood as socially constructed, the changing position of grandparents as life expectancy rises, children’s experiences shaped by class, gender and ethnicity, and changing concepts of motherhood and fatherhood.
caption: Childhood, grandparenthood and parenthood are social roles that change over time.

alt: Paper 2 is worth 60 marks, lasts 1 hour 30 minutes and is 50% of the AS and 25% of the A Level. Section A has three compulsory questions weighted towards AO1 and AO2; Section B is one 26-mark essay from two, where AO3 carries most weight.
caption: Section A tests knowledge and application; the Section B essay is where evaluation counts most.

alt: A house: the roof is 3.2, the forms families take, and inside are 4.1 gender and 4.2 age, what happens within those forms. Side notes advise learning 3.1’s three perspectives as a set and tracking which feminist strand makes which argument.
caption: 3.2 is about the forms families take; 4.1 and 4.2 are about what happens inside them.
